fields.sections.4.exchanges.1.con.words: Bowen argues that Jesus’s Luke 17 illustration assumes a slave must continue serving after fieldwork, weakening the claim that the New Testament condemns slavery.
fields.sections.4.exchanges.1.con.critique: Strongest feature: Bowen identifies the Luke 17 sequence—field labor followed by cooking, serving, and waiting—as textual pressure against the claim that Jesus condemns slavery. Principal limitation: because an illustration may draw upon a social arrangement without endorsing it, the passage’s assumed master-slave relationship cannot independently establish the conclusion that the New Testament lacks an abolitionist trajectory. Live burden: Bowen must explain why Jesus’s uncorrected use of compulsory service carries canonical significance, address the illustration’s surrounding purpose and rival readings, and show how this example answers more than one strand of Knechtle’s whole-canon case. Locked score: the fixed score of 80 fits a responsive textual counterexample whose service sequence materially advances noncondemnation, while withholding stronger credit because its doctrinal force, contextual warrant, and conclusion remain underdeveloped and somewhat overbroad.
